newsitem.title: USA: U.S. electric bills may not change in short run.
newsitem.headline: U.S. electric bills may not change in short run.

text.p: Consumers will see little change in their electric bills in the short run when local power markets are opened to competition, if states let utilities recoup all the costs of their bad past investments, U.S. Energy Information Administration said Wednesday.

But if utilities are left to shoulder their unprofitable investments, all electricity users could see rates fall from an average of 7.1 cents per kilowatthour to as low as 6.0 cents within three years, including price drops stemming from competition already underway in bulk power markets.

"In cases where policymakers grant suppliers 100 percent stranded cost recovery, average competitive prices will closely resemble regulated prices in the short term," EIA said in an analysis of electricity prices in a competitive market.

Two states moving rapidly towards competition -- California and Pennsylvania -- already plan to allow utilities to recover most of their stranded costs, which consumer groups fear will set the pattern for other states and delay the benefits of competition to homeowners and small businesses.

"Over the short term, without recovery of stranded costs, the effects of full scale competition could reduce electricity prices nationally by as much as 8 to 15 percent," Energy Department's statistical agency said.
Longer term, EIA estimated that average retail prices would fall by 13 to 21 percent from today's levels.

The drop predicted by EIA was much less than the 43 percent decrease projected in a study released last year by the conservative group Citizens for a Sound Economy and touted by lawmakers pushing to make states deregulate their markets.

EIA estimated total stranded costs for investor-owned utilities would range from $110 billion to more than $400 billion, depending on how competitive the market is and how much power plant use changes if utilities offer lower prices during off-peak periods.

It said price changes would vary from region to region, with customers in the Northwest, who enjoyed the cheapest rates on average, likely to see higher electric bills in a competitive market, and high-cost areas like New York and California likely to see the biggest price drops.
House Commerce Committee Chairman Thomas Bliley, R-Va., pushing deregulation, said the study showed benefits of increased competition.
"I'm surprised and delighted that the same Energy Information Agency which once wrongly predicted price hikes from natural gas deregulation now confirm what we've been saying all along," Bliley said.
